desc:
nums is a permutation of 0..n-1. For a starting index k build a list as follows: put nums[k] in it, then nums[nums[k]], then nums[nums[nums[k]]], and so on, stopping just before an element would be added that is already in the list.

Return the largest list length over all starting indices k.

Example: nums = [5, 4, 0, 3, 1, 6, 2]. Starting at k = 0 gives 5, 6, 2, 0 and then 5 would repeat, so the length is 4. The answer is 4.
hints: Simulating every starting index independently with a set can take O(n<sup>2</sup>) time in total. Look for work that is shared between starts.
In a permutation the list you build from k is the cycle that contains k. Starting from any member of that cycle gives the same length.
Mark indices as visited while walking. Start a new walk only from unvisited indices, and keep the maximum number of steps of a walk.
editorial: The arrows i -> nums[i] form disjoint cycles because nums is a permutation. The list built from index k contains exactly the members of the cycle through k, so the answer is the length of the longest cycle.

Scan the indices; for every index that has not been visited, walk along its cycle, marking each index and counting the steps until you meet a visited index (which will be the start of the walk). Remember the biggest count. Every index is visited once, so the time is O(n); marking can be done in place by overwriting entries, which gives O(1) extra space.
solution:
def longestNesting(nums):
    nums = list(nums)
    best = 0
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        if nums[i] >= 0:
            length = 0
            j = i
            while nums[j] >= 0:
                nxt = nums[j]
                nums[j] = -1
                j = nxt
                length += 1
            best = max(best, length)
    return best
